text: The spreadsheet has forty tabs and I'm walking through them one by one, pulling totals from each into the summary sheet. My hands move from the trackpad to the keys and back without a pause. When I finally glance at the wall clock, the afternoon has gone and the sun is off the carpet.

Columns of invoices slide past while I reconcile the last quarter against the bank export. Each mismatch gets a small note in the margin and a tick, and the next one is already on screen. Somewhere behind me the printer has finished a long job, and nobody has collected the pages.

Drafting the proposal goes in one long run, the paragraphs arriving in the order I need them. Two messages from my manager ping in the corner of the screen, and I read both without leaving the sentence I'm on. When I stop to stretch, my shoulders are stiff and the window has gone dark.

A whiteboard in the small meeting room is covered in my boxes and arrows, and the marker is nearly dry. I redraw the chain of approvals three times, each version cleaner than the last, with my back to the door. Twice a cleaning trolley rattles past the glass before I notice the room has emptied of everyone but me.

I dice the onions into a pile so fine the knife starts to sing against the board. The pan hisses when the garlic goes in, and I give it a stir, then another, then tip in the tomatoes without measuring. When I lift my head, the kitchen window is full of blue dusk and the rice has been resting for ages.

Noodles drop into the boiling pot and I don't count the minutes, just watch the steam climb toward the extractor fan. My chopsticks flick scallion and sesame into the sauce, quick as a card dealer. Only when the bowl is empty do I notice the tea beside it has gone cold and the radio has moved on to a different station.

The plum is so ripe that juice runs down my wrist before I've bitten into it. I eat standing at the sink with the tap dripping in its slow rhythm. Somewhere in the middle I stop hearing the drip, and when the stone is finally in my palm, my wrist is sticky and the dishes are still waiting.

The dough springs back against my palm each time I push it away, and I fold it over and turn it again without counting. Flour settles on the wooden board like fresh snow. The oven timer rang a while ago, and I only register it when I reach for the loaf.

The on-ramp merges me into a stream of trucks, and I slide into a gap the width of my own bumper. The road bends with the river, and the lane lines hum under the tires. When the exit sign appears, the last twelve miles are gone, leaving only a clean stretch of asphalt and the turn of the wheel.

The train rattles through the tunnel and the window turns into a black mirror with my face in it. I'm reading the paperback at speed, each sentence arriving before the last one has faded. At the next stop I lift my eyes and find half the carriage has emptied while I wasn't watching.

My legs find the rhythm before my head does, and the bike hums up the long hill with the chain ticking like a clock. Wind pushes wet leaves across the path and I dodge them without deciding to. At the bottom the office gate is in front of me, and I can't say which streets I just passed through.

White dashes come at me in a steady beat, and I keep the wheel loose with two fingers. Past midnight the dashboard glow is the only color in the cab, and the road keeps unspooling into the headlights. When the radio says it's three o'clock, I can't account for the last hour.

Pressing bulbs into the bed one after another, I stay on my knees in the dirt, the trowel handle worn smooth under my palm. Sparrows squabble in the hedge, and the soil smells of rain that hasn't come yet. When I sit back on my heels, the fence's shadow has swung right across the path.

The trail climbs through pine needles, and I stop counting switchbacks somewhere near the second ridge. My boots find roots and stones without my looking down, and a jay keeps scolding from a branch overhead. Then the trees open onto the valley, blue with haze, and I have no idea how long I've been climbing.

Waves fold over my ankles and retreat, each one pulling a little sand from under my heels. I'm crouched at the tide line sorting pale stones into a row, then sorting them again by size. A gull lands, eyes me, and leaves. The sun has slid behind the cliff, and the cold has crept up my legs before I notice.

I crouch beneath the oak, turning leaves over with a stick to check for the orange flash of a cap. The light through the canopy shifts from green to gold without my looking up. Only when my phone buzzes in my pocket do I find that an hour of the afternoon has gone into a basket of six chanterelles.

Scrubbing grout takes both my knees, and each pass turns the gray line a little whiter than before. The radio murmurs on the windowsill, and the bucket water goes cloudy, then clear, then cloudy again. When I finally wring out the rag, the bathtub gleams and I can't remember which room I started in.

Warm towels come out of the dryer in a heap, and I fold each one into thirds, then halves, my hands repeating the motion faster than I'd planned. Socks pair themselves in my palms. The basket empties, the stack on the bed climbs, and the evening light has turned orange on the wall before I look up.

I plunge my arms into the sink up to the elbow, and the water is hot enough to sting. Plates slide from my hands to the rack, each one clean before I've reached for the next. Someone calls my name from the hallway, and it takes me two tries to hear it over the running tap.

I sweep the hall in long, even strokes, the broom gathering dust into soft gray drifts against the skirting. The dog follows me from room to room, nosing the piles I've left behind. When I stop to lean on the handle, the front windows have gone dark and the streetlamps have buzzed on.

The physiotherapist counts my knee bends aloud, and after a while I stop hearing the numbers and just follow her voice down and up. Radiator pipes knock under the window of the clinic room. When she says we're finished, the clock on the wall shows that nearly half an hour has gone.

At the kitchen table I hold the spirometer's little ball up its tube, breath after breath, the way the nurse showed me. The plastic is cool against my lips, and the ball bobs and settles at each count. When the timer chirps, I find all twelve rounds are done and I never noticed the sixth.

My chin rests on the cold metal frame while the optician flips lenses before my eyes, click, click, the chart growing sharper or softer. I read the letters row by row, each line arriving before I've properly tried. When she says that's the last one, I blink and see that ten minutes have passed since she first asked me to begin.

In the warm hydrotherapy pool I walk the length of the lane with the water up to my ribs. Each stride pushes against the resistance, and my arms cut the surface in wide slow arcs. The instructor's whistle sounds from the far end, and I'm already at the wall before I think to turn.

My nephew builds a tower of wooden blocks on the rug, and I hand him each one, still warm from my palm. We barely talk. He hums to himself, I hum back, and the afternoon light slides across the floorboards. When his mom calls us for lunch, the tower has reached the height of his arm, and I hadn't noticed the sun move.

Around the kitchen table my friends slap down cards and laugh at the same jokes they laughed at last year. I keep the trick count on the back of a napkin, my pen moving steadily while the bowl of chips empties. Someone asks what time it is, and it's already past midnight.

My sister braids my daughter's hair on the back step, her fingers quick and sure, strands going over and under in a tight rhythm. A neighbor's cat watches from the top of the fence. Nobody speaks for a long while, and the shadows of the washing lines stretch to the gate before my sister tugs the last tie into place.

Three cousins and I are repainting my grandmother's front room, and the rollers slap the wall in long overlapping stripes. Someone's playlist keeps changing songs, and nobody bothers to pick a new one. When the last corner is done and I climb down the ladder, the paint has dried on my wrists and it's already dark outside.

The problem set is a page of integrals, and I work down the list, each substitution unlocking the next line without a pause. The pencil scratches, the desk lamp hums, and my eraser has gone soft from use. The library lights flicker twice before I look up, and by then my margin is full.

My Latin translation is spread across the desk, and the verbs fall into place as I read, each ablative leading me to the next clause. Rain ticks on the skylight. The sandwich I set beside the book at noon is still wrapped, and I haven't touched it.

At the lab bench I pipette clear liquid into each row of the plate, counting drops under my breath without losing my place. The fume hood hums, and the wall timer ticks down toward the color change I'm watching for. When my labmate asks if I've eaten, I see that I haven't since the morning.

The flashcards fan across my bed, and I flip them faster than I can say the answers aloud. Pencil shavings collect on the sheet in a neat little pile. Only when my roommate switches the overhead light on do I see the window has gone black and I've been at it since dinner.

My feet strike the track in an even pattern, and my breath settles into a count I don't have to think about. Sprinklers hiss across the infield, and the stands are empty except for a man walking his bicycle. Lap after lap goes by, and when the coach calls that I'm done, I'm already halfway around another loop.

I push off the wall and glide, my arms cutting the water in long arcs while the lane line bobs beside me. Bubbles stream from my nose in a steady beat. Somewhere around the fortieth length I stop counting and breathe on every turn, the chlorine sharp at the back of my throat, until the lifeguard blows the whistle for the end of the session.

My fingers find each hold before my eyes have properly picked it out, and my feet shift up the wall while chalk dust drifts down. The gym music thumps somewhere below. I'm three meters up, then six, and only when my forearms start to burn do I notice I've climbed past the blue route marker.

On the mat I move from one pose into the next, and the breath carries me through the order without my planning it. The studio's wooden floor creaks under the fan. A strand of hair sticks to my cheek, and I leave it there. When the teacher rings the chime, I find my palms pressed together and the windows have gone gray.

The needle slides in and out of the blue cotton, each stitch lying flat beside the last as my thumb presses the fold. The sewing machine's foot treadles along the seam. I've pinned the hem twice, and then I stop measuring altogether. When I bite the thread, the skirt is finished and my shoulders ache from the hunch.

The plane shaves a curl of pale pine off the edge of the board, and the smell of resin fills the shed. I run my palm along the surface and go back to the plane. Shavings pile at my boots. Only when the light through the gap in the door has shifted off the bench do I look up and see the joint fits.

My hands are black with grease as I thread the chain back over the sprocket, turning the crank slowly to check that the links sit true. The bike stand creaks. A wrench lies on the rag beside me, and I reach for the next bolt without looking. When my phone buzzes with a message, the light has drained from the garage door's gap.

The wheel spins fast under my hands, and the clay rises into a tall, narrow wall. My fingers press inward, the wall thins, then steadies. A thin ribbon of water runs down my wrists onto the apron. When I take my hands away, the vase is standing straight and I've been at the wheel for two hours.

I push the cart down the produce aisle, pressing each peach's shoulder with my thumb before it goes into the bag, then on to the next. The shelves hum with cold air. A child two aisles over points at the bright cereal boxes, and I've already moved on to the herbs. At the checkout, every item on my list has a line through it.

The screws come in tiny tubs with labels I scan quickly, matching each thread to the drawing on my phone. The aisles smell of oil and cut wood. I pick two, then a third in a slightly different size, and find the bolt I came for without asking anyone. When I finally turn around, the store's clock says closing time.

The queue barely moves, but I'm sorting my parcels on the counter into stacks while the clerk weighs them, one label after another. The tape gun clicks at a steady rhythm. When my number finally comes up, the queue behind me has grown to twelve, and I hadn't heard it grow.

At the flea market I turn over a box of old brass keys and sort them by teeth and weight on the trestle table. The vendor's radio plays oldies, and a man asks what I'm buying. I answer without looking up. When the sun reaches the far end of the market and the stalls begin to pack up, my bag is heavy and I've hardly looked at the other tables.

Two hours into the ferry crossing, the wind keeps flinging spray across the deck while I sketch the coastline in my notebook. The lines come quickly: the headland, the gulls, the rocks breaking the swell. A deckhand taps the rail beside me to say we're docking, and I realize the engines have been silent for a while.

I'm chasing street names in a language I only half read, my finger tracing the map as the tram rattles past. Each turn brings a new smell of bread and diesel. I stop for a sandwich, then a second one, without asking myself why. The shop owner is lowering his shutters when I finally check my watch.

I fold the tent poles into their bag while the car engine idles and cool morning air comes through the open hatch. Everything fits with a little push and some rearranging, the way it always does on the third try. When my partner calls from the driver's seat, I wave once and realize we've been loading for forty minutes.

The gate board flips over to our flight while I'm still tapping out the last paragraph of my travel notes. The terminal hum softens under the announcements, and a rolling suitcase clicks past. I've been writing since we landed, and when the boarding call comes, my pen has filled three pages I hardly remember writing.

My left hand walks the bass line while my right hand weaves the melody above it, the notes spilling out of the upright piano with the window open. I stop at the end of a phrase, turn back, and play it again more softly. A breeze lifts the curtain by the radiator. When I lift my fingers, the light on the keys has gone amber.

I load the brush with thick cobalt and drag it across the canvas in one long stroke, the paint thinning as it runs. A bead of water rolls off the palette knife. My sleeve has picked up a smear of yellow. I add a few flecks of white along the top edge and step back, and the studio has grown dim around the easel.

My thumb finds the groove of the riff, and the chords roll out before I've named them. Each bar goes by, the strings sharp under my fingertips and the amp humming behind me. A car passes outside, and I don't look up. When I finally set the guitar on its stand, the streetlight glows through the blind and my calluses sting.

The needles click through purl and knit rows, the gray wool sliding off my index finger. Each stitch lands in its place without my counting. The yarn ball has rolled off the arm of the chair, and I haven't reached for it. When I hold up the sleeve, it's already longer than the pattern asks for.

I rename a variable in one file, and the change ripples through four others, and I follow each ripple without checking my notes. The terminal scrolls past in green and white. When I finally scroll back to the top, the window has gone dark and my dinner is cold on the sill.

Dragging the curve point upward, I watch the shadows lift a little more with each tweak. I move the sliders in tiny steps, the harbor photo sharpening one notch at a time. The bus pulls away outside the window while I'm still on the same picture. When I look up, the lights across the street are on.

The inbox counts down from two hundred and forty as I clear it, archiving, replying, filing into folders in a steady beat. My fingers tap the keys without searching for them. The reply templates save a few keystrokes at a time. A colleague's out-of-office message pops up, and I'm already on the next one before I finish reading it.

I'm moving old photos onto the new laptop one folder at a time, and the progress bar creeps along at its own pace. My brother's wedding pictures scroll past, and I sort them by date, dragging each file into place. When the transfer finishes, the room is brighter than it was when I started.
